title: Do not buy optional rewards with critical HP
situation: When already below full HP and several combats remain before the boss, evaluate HP-cost events as a major combat resource rather than as free gold or upgrades.
lesson: Decline optional HP-loss events unless their reward is essential to the run’s immediate survival plan. The gold from Gather Gold and the random upgrades from Enter were not worth repeatedly reducing the HP buffer before the boss.
evidence_points: At Floor 4, HP was 68/80 and Gather Gold was chosen, reducing HP to 57/80.
At Floor 5, HP was 57/80 and Enter was chosen, reducing HP to 41/80.
After those choices, combat logs reached 29/80 at Floor 6 and 24/80 at Floor 7.
reasoning: The two optional events removed 27 HP before later fights, and the subsequent combat losses left the run dependent on scarce healing. This made the later boss approach much less forgiving.

title: Prioritize a second heal when the boss approach is fragile
situation: At a campfire before the Act 1 boss, if HP remains substantially below maximum after an earlier rest and there are no saved potions, healing is usually more valuable than a marginal upgrade.
lesson: After recovering from a low-HP route, continue healing at the next available campfire when the upcoming combats are still likely to consume the buffer. Do not automatically smith at around half HP when the boss is close.
evidence_points: Floor 8 used a rest at 24/80 HP and recovered to 48/80.
At Floor 10, with 48/80 HP, smith was chosen instead of rest and Bash was upgraded.
The run then reached the Floor 15 rest at 11/80, recovered only to 35/80, and entered the Slime Boss combat at 35/80.
reasoning: The smith produced an upgrade, but the following fights reduced HP far faster than the run could recover. The final boss therefore started with only 35 HP and died after reaching a 7-HP state, indicating that preserving a larger pre-boss HP buffer was more urgent than the additional upgrade.

title: At critical HP, convert unused energy into immediate block
situation: When entering a turn at very low HP with no block and defensive cards legally playable, especially before enemies can attack.
lesson: Prioritize surviving the current enemy cycle over marginal damage: play available Defends or other mitigation before ending the turn, unless lethal damage is clearly guaranteed.
evidence_points: The final combat began at 19/80 HP and 0 Block; after playing Bash+ and Headbutt, the agent ended Turn 1 with three Defends still in hand and all three were legal alternatives.
On Turn 2, both enemies had attack-related intents while the player was still at 19 HP, requiring Impervious to avoid immediate danger.
reasoning: The first turn established a dangerous zero-block state despite legal defensive actions, and the next turn confirms that enemy attacks were an immediate concern. At 19 HP, preserving health was more important than spending the whole opening turn on damage setup.

title: Stop adding redundant attacks when attrition is already severe
situation: After several combats have caused substantial HP loss and the deck already contains many attack cards, particularly when a reward offers defensive or utility alternatives.
lesson: Favor mitigation, draw, exhaust synergy, or other survivability tools over another ordinary attack when the deck's damage is already adequate; make the deck better at preventing the HP loss that limits future fights.
evidence_points: The final 23-card deck contains three Strikes, Bash+, two Headbutts, Reckless Charge, Pummel, two Sword Boomerangs, Hemokinesis, Thunderclap, and other damage cards, alongside only four Defends and a limited set of defensive tools.
The run's HP repeatedly declined during Act 1 and Act 2: it was 52/80 after the early Act 1 fights, 20/80 after the Hexaghost fight, and 19/80 before the final Act 2 combat.
At Act 1 Floor 11, the reward alternatives included Sentinel, but Sword Boomerang was chosen; at Act 1 Floor 2, Sentinel and Dark Embrace were also alternatives to the chosen Pummel.
reasoning: The exact alternatives were not always strictly better, but the repeated attack additions and large HP losses indicate that future rewards should be evaluated for survivability rather than continuing to increase damage density. The deck did eventually acquire Impervious, Feel No Pain+, and Disarm, but the low HP shows that defensive development came too slowly or too inconsistently.

title: At critical HP, reassess the damage race instead of defaulting to block
situation: When HP is already near lethal, the boss is below half health, and several defensive cards are available alongside legal attacks or debuffs.
lesson: Explicitly compare whether another defensive turn can realistically survive the next attack; if not, prefer the strongest legal damage or vulnerability line. Do not automatically spend all energy on multiple Defends merely because the enemy intends to attack.
evidence_points: On Turn 21, the player had 10 HP and 3 energy while The Guardian had 76 HP, 9 Block, and ATTACK intent; Strike, Thunderclap, and three Defends were all legal.
The chosen sequence played Defend three times, ending at 10 Block with the Guardian still at 76 HP.
The run ended in the same boss combat, with the final recorded Guardian HP still 76/240.
reasoning: This sequence consumed the entire turn without reducing the Guardian's HP, leaving the fight unresolved while the player was already at critical health. Exact incoming damage is unavailable, so this is a race-management hypothesis rather than proof that a specific attack line would have won.

title: Evaluate consistency before taking a second expensive finisher
situation: After already obtaining a high-cost finisher, especially when a shop offers card removal or when the deck still contains many starter attacks.
lesson: Before adding another copy of the same expensive payoff, favor removal or cheaper support unless the deck clearly needs redundancy and can reliably provide energy or draw. This helps the key finisher appear in a more functional deck.
evidence_points: The shop offered card removal for 75 gold and Fiend Fire for 151 gold; the run bought Fiend Fire and later had only 1 gold.
A second Fiend Fire was taken as a reward at Floor 13.
The final 18-card deck contained two Fiend Fire+ cards and four Strike cards.
reasoning: The run invested in duplicate expensive finishers while retaining four starter Strikes, suggesting a consistency tradeoff. The trajectory does not prove that the second Fiend Fire was strictly incorrect, but it supports checking removal and deck smoothness before taking redundant high-cost cards.

title: Use healthy campfires to upgrade the central payoff
situation: When reaching a campfire with enough HP to survive upcoming fights and a key card that substantially improves the deck when upgraded.
lesson: Preserve campfire flexibility: rest when current HP is meaningfully low, but smith when healthy, prioritizing the deck's central finisher or scaling card. This run's pattern of resting at risk and upgrading Fiend Fire at high HP is worth repeating.
evidence_points: At Floor 8 the player had 46/80 HP and chose to rest, reaching 70/80 HP afterward.
At Floor 10, with 70/80 HP, the player chose to smith Fiend Fire.
At Floor 15, with 80/80 HP, the player again chose to smith Fiend Fire; the final deck contains two Fiend Fire+ cards.
reasoning: The decisions matched the immediate survival need while using later high-HP campfires for impactful upgrades. This supported reaching the boss at full health and produced a clearly upgraded core payoff.

title: Defend first when low HP and facing an attack
situation: When HP is already low, the enemy intends to attack, and a Defend is legally playable, especially if the hand contains no immediate lethal line.
lesson: Do not spend the turn on marginal damage while leaving yourself at zero block. In the Guardian fight on Turn 6, prioritize Defend or another available block card before attacks; preserving one extra turn is more valuable than modest damage when already near death.
evidence_points: Turn 6 began at 26/80 HP with 0 block, The Guardian had ATTACK intent, and Defend was a legal alternative.
The agent chose Iron Wave and then Bash instead, ending the decision sequence with 0 block; the next logged state showed HP reduced to 11/80.
At Turn 7, the agent was still at 11/80 HP and continued attacking with Carnage and Iron Wave rather than establishing a defensive buffer.
reasoning: The logged states show a clear deterioration from 26 HP to 11 HP after choosing attacks despite a legal Defend against an attack intent. Exact incoming damage is unavailable, but the causal pattern is unambiguous: the choice left no block and made the subsequent turns much less recoverable.

title: Treat curse-for-gold events as a real deck cost
situation: When an event offers substantial gold for adding a curse and there is no confirmed near-term removal opportunity or curse synergy.
lesson: Prefer avoiding the curse unless the gold has a clear, high-value use and the deck can reliably absorb the dead draw. A curse that remains in the deck can directly reduce hand quality during an important boss fight.
evidence_points: At Floor 13 and 48/80 HP, the agent chose to gain 175 gold and become cursed with Doubt.
Doubt remained in the final 19-card deck.
During the Guardian fight on Turn 5, Doubt occupied a hand slot and was selected while the player was at 26/80 HP.
reasoning: The event permanently exchanged deck quality for gold, and the resulting curse was visibly present in a critical low-HP boss turn. This does not prove the event choice alone caused the loss, but it supports treating similar curse offers more cautiously when there is no documented removal plan.

title: Treat sustained mid-act HP loss as an emergency
situation: When HP has dropped substantially during Act 1 and a campfire becomes available, especially after several combats have already caused damage.
lesson: Switch from upgrade greed to survival planning earlier: take healing at the next available campfire whenever continued combat would leave the run entering the Act boss at dangerously low HP.
evidence_points: HP was 59/85 after the Lagavulin fight on floor 7, then declined to 33/85 on floor 12, 10/85 on floor 13, and 7/85 on floor 14.
The only later REST_DECISION was on floor 15, where rest was chosen, but the Guardian combat still began with only 32/85 HP.
During the Guardian fight, HP fell from 32/85 at the first logged combat state to 15/85 on turn 4 and 2/85 on turn 5.
reasoning: The trajectory shows a prolonged attrition trend that was not repaired until the run was already nearly dead. Resting at floor 15 was correct, but the resulting boss starting HP was still too low to absorb even a few attacks, so future decisions should treat this level of attrition as a survival crisis earlier.

title: Stop taking every card reward once the deck has a functioning core
situation: When several rewards have already been accepted and later choices are merely situational additions rather than clear improvements to consistency or survivability.
lesson: Use Skip more often and require each new card to solve a specific deck problem; otherwise preserve draw quality and avoid diluting the core plan with additional setup cards.
evidence_points: The run selected a card at every listed permanent CARD_REWARD decision, including rewards on floors 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14; Skip was never chosen.

The final deck contained 21 cards, including five Strikes, four Defends, and many separate scaling, exhaust, and utility cards such as Inflame+, Spot Weakness, Limit Break, Corruption, Feel No Pain, Warcry, and True Grit.
The deck still produced prolonged and damaging combats: HP fell to 53 after Lagavulin, 27 after the floor 12 combat, and 4 after the floor 13 combat.
reasoning: The individual picks were not all demonstrably wrong, and the trajectory does not prove that any one card caused the loss. However, accepting every reward created a broad 21-card list while the run continued to take heavy combat damage, supporting a reusable rule to skip marginal cards and protect consistency once a viable plan exists.

title: Prioritize boss-entry survivability when already damaged
situation: At the campfire immediately before an Act boss, especially when below full HP and without a reliable potion buffer.
lesson: Compare an upgrade against the concrete value of healing; when entering the boss at substantially reduced HP, favor resting unless the upgrade is very likely to prevent more damage than the heal provides.
evidence_points: On Floor 15, the run had 57/80 HP and chose to smith Uppercut rather than rest immediately before The Guardian.
The Guardian fight began at 57/80 HP and the player reached 1 HP by Turn 11.
The final build had no potions remaining.
reasoning: The upgrade may have improved the deck, but the run had little health margin for the boss and no remaining potion buffer. The subsequent fight consumed nearly all remaining HP, so preserving boss-entry health should receive more weight in this situation.

title: Take safe damage before setup against a defending boss
situation: When the enemy is defending, you have some block, and an attack is legally playable with your remaining energy.
lesson: Prefer the available attack before using draw/exhaust setup cards unless the setup has an immediate, clearly superior payoff. Do not spend the only energy on setup when the enemy is not attacking and a safe hit is available.
evidence_points: On Turn 9, The Guardian had 161/240 HP, 0 block, and Intent DEFEND; with 1 energy and 16 player block, Strike+ was legal alongside Burning Pact+.
The chosen action was Burning Pact+, leaving 0 energy, followed by selecting Strike+ rather than playing it.
On Turn 10, the player was at 6 HP with 0 block while The Guardian had Intent ATTACK, and the player eventually reached 1 HP on Turn 11.
reasoning: Turn 9 offered a low-risk opportunity to deal damage because the boss was defending and the player already had block. Choosing setup instead removed the immediate attack opportunity and left the next turn to be played under attack pressure, contributing to the very narrow survival margin.

title: Skip more marginal attack rewards
situation: When Act 1 rewards offer another generic attack after the deck already has several attacks and some damage coverage.
lesson: Use Skip more often to preserve draw consistency. In particular, avoid taking duplicate or low-impact attacks unless they address a clear current need; a smaller deck makes key defensive and damage cards appear more reliably in difficult fights.
evidence_points: The run accepted nine permanent card rewards, including Clothesline, Twin Strike, two Pommel Strikes, Hemokinesis, and Second Wind.
The final deck contained 21 cards, including four Strikes, four Defends, two Pommel Strikes, and several other attacks.
Hexaghost reached the late fight with 31 HP while the player had only 9 HP, showing that the accumulated deck and combat plan did not produce a sufficiently decisive boss race.
reasoning: The trajectory does not prove that any single reward caused the loss, but repeatedly accepting rewards—including a second Pommel Strike—created a relatively large Act 1 deck. Future runs should be more selective when a reward does not materially improve the deck's immediate plan.

title: Reassess the damage-versus-survival line at critical HP
situation: When HP is in the single digits, the boss is still alive, and several attack and block lines are simultaneously legal.
lesson: Do not automatically spend the whole turn on partial blocking. Compare every legal sequence for either a near-lethal attack or enough block to survive, especially when the boss is already below roughly one-third health; at minimum, explicitly evaluate attack options such as Bash or Twin Strike before committing to Shrug It Off plus Defend.
evidence_points: On turn 11, with 9 HP, Hexaghost at 31 HP, and 3 energy, the legal alternatives included Defend, Strike, Shrug It Off, Twin Strike, and later Bash; the chosen line was Shrug It Off, Defend, then Twin Strike.
That line left Hexaghost at 21 HP and the player at 9 HP with 9 block, after which the run ended with Hexaghost still alive at 16 HP.
One turn earlier, at 13 HP against Hexaghost at 54 HP, the player chose Defend before playing both Pommel Strikes and ended the turn with only 5 block; the next logged turn began at 9 HP.
reasoning: The exact incoming damage and best counterfactual line are not fully recoverable, so this is not proof that a particular card would have won. However, the logged states show repeated turns where the player made only incremental progress while approaching lethal danger; future play should explicitly prioritize either a verified kill or a survival threshold rather than defaulting to mixed low-impact lines.

title: Against Gremlin Nob, minimize unnecessary skills
situation: When fighting Gremlin Nob, especially after his attack pattern begins, prefer legal attacks or ending the turn over extra Skill plays unless the block is essential.
lesson: Track Nob's strength gain from Skills and avoid chaining Shrug It Off, Intimidate, Defend, or Defend+ when an attack is available. In this fight, after Immolate+ left 1 energy, Strike was legal but Shrug It Off was chosen; on turn 3, two Shrugs were played before Strike; and on turn 4, Defend+ was chosen while Strikes were legal.
evidence_points: Turn 2 after Immolate+: at 1 energy, both Shrug It Off and Strike were legal, but Shrug It Off was chosen.
Turn 3: Shrug It Off was played twice before Strike while Strike remained a legal alternative.
Turn 4: with Gremlin Nob attacking, Defend+ was chosen even though two Strikes were legal; the fight later reached player HP 18/72.
reasoning: The logged decisions show repeated optional Skill plays rather than a single unavoidable defensive turn. Since Gremlin Nob punishes Skill usage with strength, this pattern makes future incoming attacks increasingly dangerous and was a more causal problem than the final low-HP state.

title: Avoid overloading the early deck with defensive Skills
situation: During Act 1 card rewards, particularly before an elite or boss, choose additional damage or utility over another defensive Skill when the deck already has basic defense.
lesson: Do not repeatedly take Shrug It Off and Intimidate just because they are reliable cards. The run took Intimidate over Iron Wave or Headbutt and took Shrug It Off twice; future rewards should more often select attacks, damage scaling, or skip when the deck is already defense-heavy.
evidence_points: At floor 2, Intimidate was chosen over Iron Wave and Headbutt.
At floor 5, Shrug It Off was chosen over Clothesline and Armaments, after Shrug It Off had already been taken earlier.
The final 13-card deck contains four Defends, two Shrug It Offs, and Intimidate, alongside only three Strikes, Bash, Immolate+, and Blood for Blood as attacks.
reasoning: The reward history and final build both show a concentration of defensive Skills. That made the deck less suitable for a Nob fight, where playing many Skills is especially costly, so future Act 1 rewards should preserve a stronger damage-to-defense balance.

title: Use the campfire to secure HP before a high-risk fight
situation: When a dangerous upcoming fight is possible and HP is well below maximum, compare the value of an upgrade against entering the fight with a substantially larger survival buffer.
lesson: At 53/72 HP with no recorded potion inventory, do not automatically smith. Resting was available at floor 6, and the run entered the Gremlin Nob fight still at 53/72 before falling to 18/72 in the logged combat; in a similar situation, favor rest unless the upgrade is clearly necessary.
evidence_points: At floor 6, HP was 53/72 and both rest and smith were legal; smith was chosen to upgrade Immolate.
The next logged combat began at HP 53/72 against Gremlin Nob.
During the Nob fight, the last logged player HP was 18/72 while Nob remained at 41/85.
reasoning: The trajectory does not prove that resting would have guaranteed victory, but it shows that the upgrade-focused choice provided no additional HP buffer before the run's lethal fight. This is a useful risk-management adjustment when the next combat may punish a skill-heavy or incomplete deck.

title: Prioritize mitigation when several enemies are attacking
situation: When HP is already low, block is zero, and multiple enemies show attack intents.
lesson: Do not automatically spend the whole turn on area damage. First compare an available defensive line such as Power Through or Iron Wave against the incoming threat; use Whirlwind only when the resulting damage and remaining survivability justify ending the turn with no block.
evidence_points: On turn 2 of the final fight, HP was 27/77, block was 0, all three Cultists intended to attack, and Power Through and Iron Wave were legal alternatives.
Whirlwind was chosen with 4 energy, leaving turn 3 at 9/77 HP and 0 block while two Cultists still had 31 and 29 HP.
reasoning: The logged sequence shows that the all-out attack reduced enemy HP but left the player exposed to a large combined attack and immediately created a critical-HP state. The same decision offered defensive alternatives, so future play should explicitly evaluate survival before maximizing damage.

title: Sequence defense before offense at lethal HP
situation: When HP is in the single digits and the hand contains both attacks and block, especially with enemies attacking.
lesson: Play enough defense before committing to expensive damage. Avoid using a self-damaging attack merely to finish a nearly dead enemy unless it is necessary for survival or creates a clearly decisive kill.
evidence_points: On turn 4 of the final fight, HP was 7/77, block was 0, both remaining Cultists intended to attack, and Ghostly Armor, Shrug It Off, and Immolate were all legal.
Immolation was played first; after Armaments+ and Ghostly Armor+, the player still reached the next turn at 1/77 HP.
On turn 3, Hemokinesis was used to kill a Cultist at 1 HP while the player had 9 HP and 13 block, reducing HP to 7.
reasoning: These choices repeatedly traded HP for damage while already near death. The trajectory does not prove a unique winning alternative, but it supports a reusable rule to treat single-digit HP as a defensive emergency and to sequence block before attacks whenever possible.

title: Stop adding redundant cards once the deck is already large
situation: After acquiring a functional damage-and-block core, especially when reward options repeat effects already present.
lesson: Prefer skipping marginal rewards or pursuing removal/quality improvements over adding redundant copies. Keep the deck compact enough that key defensive cards are drawn reliably.
evidence_points: The final permanent deck contained 32 cards, including two Power Through cards and two Ghostly Armor cards, one of each upgraded.
Power Through was taken in two separate Act 2 rewards, and Ghostly Armor+ was taken at floor 20 before another Ghostly Armor was taken at floor 28.
The final combat opened with only Strike and Seeing Red in hand, despite the deck containing substantial defensive and offensive tools.
reasoning: The repeated additions increased the deck without guaranteeing access to the needed defensive cards at the critical moment. Once the deck already had multiple strong tools, skipping redundant rewards would have improved draw consistency and reduced dead or situational hands.

title: Prioritize immediate defense over more scaling when survival is already strained
situation: When HP has been falling across combats and a reward offers both a defensive card and another scaling or damage card.
lesson: Prefer cards that immediately improve block, draw, or hand quality over additional scaling unless the deck is already surviving reliably. In particular, do not automatically choose Limit Break-type scaling when a defensive option such as Shrug It Off is available.
evidence_points: At Floor 11, the reward offered Shrug It Off and Limit Break; Limit Break was chosen.
The final deck contained Inflame and upgraded Limit Break, but only four Defends plus Shrug It Off, True Grit, Intimidate, and Warcry as clear defensive or defensive-support cards.
The Guardian fight later reached HP 21 on Turn 12 and HP 2 on Turn 14.
reasoning: The run already had multiple ways to increase damage, while its HP trajectory and final combat show that surviving incoming attacks was the limiting problem. This makes the defensive reward the more robust choice in similar situations.

title: At critical HP, do not spend surplus block energy on marginal damage
situation: When at very low HP against an enemy showing an attack intent and the current block is not clearly sufficient.
lesson: Calculate whether the current block safely covers the attack before attacking. If it does not, use the available Defend effects instead of converting the remaining energy into a Strike or other low-impact attack.
evidence_points: On Turn 15 at HP 2 with The Guardian showing ATTACK, after playing Shrug It Off the agent had 8 Block and 2 Energy, then chose Defend followed by Strike.
At that exact decision, both Defend and Strike were legal alternatives.
On Turn 16, the agent was still at HP 2 with 0 Block and again faced an ATTACK intent.
reasoning: The Turn 15 Strike provided limited progress while leaving only 13 Block before an attack at 2 HP. Because the exact incoming damage is unavailable, the claim is conditional rather than certain, but at this survival threshold the safer default is to add block unless coverage is already established.

title: Evaluate the final campfire for boss survivability, not only damage scaling
situation: At the last campfire before an Act boss, especially after hallway fights have caused substantial HP loss.
lesson: Before upgrading an offensive scaling card, compare it against the value of healing or upgrading a defensive option. If the boss plan depends on surviving several attack turns, entering with more HP or stronger defense can be worth more than increasing an already adequate damage engine.
evidence_points: At Floor 15, immediately before the Guardian, the agent had 68/80 HP and chose smith, upgrading Limit Break.
The Guardian combat then reduced the player to 21 HP by Turn 12 and 2 HP by Turn 14.
The run ended with The Guardian still at 15/240 HP.
reasoning: The final upgrade improved scaling, but the boss fight was decided by survival margins rather than lack of access to damage. The repeated drop to critical HP indicates that the final campfire decision should have explicitly prioritized boss endurance.

title: Prioritize immediate mitigation at critical HP
situation: When facing an attack intent with low HP and multiple defensive cards available, especially before the enemy has been weakened enough to guarantee a kill.
lesson: Treat survival as the first constraint: prefer legal block or damage-reduction plays over damage/setup when one more hit may end the fight. In particular, do not spend the entire first turn on Immolate against Book of Stabbing while leaving zero block unless the resulting damage race is clearly favorable.
evidence_points: On Turn 1 against Book of Stabbing, HP was 41/86, the enemy intent was ATTACK, and Defend was legal, but Immolate was played for all 2 energy, leaving 0 block.
By Turn 2 HP had fallen to 19/86; despite two Defends and True Grit being legal, Thunderclap and Disarm were chosen before True Grit, and the run reached Turn 3 at 14/86.

On Turn 4 HP was 10/86 with Book of Stabbing still at 113 HP, yet the turn still began with a defensive choice followed by only one attack, showing that the fight had already become an unfavorable damage race.
reasoning: The exact incoming damage is not logged, so the precise counterfactual is uncertain, but the sequence clearly shows that early damage/setup choices failed to preserve enough HP to sustain the fight. A future agent should switch to a survival-first policy earlier when the enemy is attacking and HP is already in the danger zone.

title: Use high-HP campfires for upgrades rather than small heals
situation: At a campfire where current HP is already reasonably high and there is no documented immediate need for a larger health buffer.
lesson: Reserve resting for genuinely dangerous HP totals; when already around three-quarters health, prefer smithing unless a specific upcoming fight makes the extra HP more valuable than an upgrade.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 7, resting from 33/80 to 57/80 was a substantial recovery and was appropriate for the low-HP state.
At Act 1 Floor 11, the run rested at 62/80 and only recovered to 71/80, trading an available smith opportunity for a relatively modest heal.
At Act 1 Floor 15, the run was at 78/80 and used the campfire to recall the Ruby Key, so no upgrade was obtained there either.
reasoning: The contrast between the necessary low-HP rest and the later high-HP rest indicates that at least one campfire was used for limited healing rather than permanent deck improvement. More upgrades before the Act 1 boss and Act 2 could improve both damage efficiency and defensive consistency.

title: Preserve shop resources for immediate survival when HP is falling
situation: When entering an Act 2 shop at moderate or low HP with several dangerous combats still ahead and limited gold.
lesson: Evaluate purchases by whether they stabilize the next fights, and avoid spending nearly all remaining gold on long-term value if doing so leaves no potion or defensive fallback. Immediate survivability should generally outrank an expensive scaling purchase when the run is already losing HP each floor.
evidence_points: At Act 2 Floor 20, the run entered the shop at 54/80 HP and bought Inflame, then removed a Strike, then bought Feed for 151 gold, ending with only 21 gold.
The shop offered Blood Potion, Liquid Memories, and Strength Potion, but no potion was purchased.
After the shop, HP fell to 28/83 after the next combat and then to 16/86 after the following combat, leaving the run dependent on a later rest before Book of Stabbing.
reasoning: The trajectory does not prove that a particular potion would have saved the run, but the spending sequence left almost no emergency resources while HP continued to decline. In similar low-HP Act 2 shops, the purchase plan should first secure the next few combats rather than maximize longer-term scaling.

title: Respect attack turns before spending all energy on damage
situation: When an enemy is attacking and defensive cards are legal, especially after the player has already lost substantial HP.
lesson: Reserve enough energy for meaningful block instead of automatically converting the whole turn into damage. In the final fight, after Bash+ was played into Mad Gremlin, the legal Defend cards should have been seriously prioritized over Pommel Strike+ while Gremlin Leader was attacking.
evidence_points: On turn 2 of the Gremlin Leader fight, the player had 54 HP, 0 Block, 3 Energy, two Defends in hand, and Gremlin Leader had Intent ATTACK.
The chosen sequence was Bash+ followed by Pommel Strike+, leaving no block; the next logged state showed the player at 27 HP.
reasoning: The state explicitly offered defensive alternatives at the same decision where the Leader was attacking. The subsequent 27-HP loss shows that the all-out attack sequence created the pivotal survival deficit, even though the exact incoming damage is not inferred from the intent alone.

title: Keep required keys when pursuing the Heart
situation: When the strategic objective is an Act 4 attempt and an event offers a colored key versus a relic.
lesson: Take the Sapphire Key rather than the linked relic unless there is a deliberate decision not to pursue Act 4. Do not trade away a required key for incremental relic value early in the run.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 9, the agent chose to obtain Tiny Chest and give up the Sapphire Key.
The run ended with ruby=False, emerald=False, and sapphire=False.
reasoning: The trajectory confirms that the Sapphire Key was explicitly relinquished and was never recovered. This did not cause the Act 2 death directly, but it permanently removed the possibility of completing the three-key requirement during this run.

title: Continue skipping marginal rewards once the deck has its core tools
situation: When a reward offers situational or redundant cards and the current deck already contains reliable damage, defense, and scaling.
lesson: Prefer skipping weak additions over filling the deck. The run made several selective skips, and that discipline should be retained rather than taking every available reward.
evidence_points: The agent skipped the Act 1 Floor 10 reward rather than taking Cleave, Body Slam, or Havoc.
The agent also skipped the Act 2 Floor 22 reward rather than taking Dropkick, Body Slam+, or Flex+.
The final permanent deck contained 23 cards, including upgraded Shrug It Off, Fiend Fire, and Pommel Strike alongside scaling cards such as Inflame and Demon Form.
reasoning: The recorded skips show useful restraint, while the final deck already contained substantial damage, block, and scaling tools. Repeating this selective approach can preserve draw quality and avoid adding cards that are not clearly better than skipping.

title: Do not overpay to finish an almost-dead target
situation: When an enemy is at very low HP and multiple enemies remain, especially when the player is already low on HP.
lesson: Use the cheapest legal lethal option, then spend the remaining energy on card draw, meaningful damage to another threat, or defense. Avoid using a 2-cost attack followed by another attack on a target with only 2 HP unless that sequence provides an important defensive benefit.
evidence_points: On turn 2 of the final combat, Fat Gremlin had only 2 HP, but Bash was played first, followed by Iron Wave on the same 2-HP enemy.
After Iron Wave, Shrug It Off was played and the turn ended with Battle Trance still shown as a legal alternative at 0 energy.
The player entered that turn at 26/74 HP, while Gremlin Leader had an attack intent, so preserving energy for useful draw or threat management was especially valuable.
reasoning: The logged state shows that the nearly dead Fat Gremlin consumed three energy worth of attacks while the other enemies remained largely untouched. This sequencing reduced access to useful cards before the next dangerous turn and contributed to entering turn 3 at only 12 HP.

title: Commit earlier to the strongest deck engine instead of accumulating mixed packages
situation: After obtaining a premium attack or a clear engine such as Corruption plus exhaust support, when later rewards are merely playable rather than directly improving that plan.
lesson: Prefer skipping marginal cards and preserve a compact deck whose cards reinforce the established engine. In particular, avoid continuing to add loosely connected scaling, self-damage, and attack cards when the deck already has an exhaust/block plan.
evidence_points: The final deck contained 27 cards, retained five Strikes, and mixed Corruption, Dark Embrace, two True Grits, Power Through+, Fire Breathing, Combust, Flex, Perfected Strike, Rampage, and several large attacks.
Early rewards added Flex and Combust, while later rewards added Perfected Strike, Fire Breathing, Rampage, and Iron Wave; only one listed card reward was skipped, the Act 2 Floor 20 reward.
The deck did eventually contain a strong exhaust core: Corruption, Dark Embrace, True Grit+, True Grit, Power Through+, and Impervious.
reasoning: The final build shows a valuable Corruption/exhaust foundation, but also many cards from separate plans and several basic Strikes still occupying draws. Future runs should treat that established engine as the selection filter and skip cards that do not materially improve it, increasing consistency and reducing HP loss from weak draws.

title: Keep using low-HP rests before pivotal fights
situation: When HP has fallen substantially below maximum and the next route segment or boss requires reliable combat performance.
lesson: Choose healing when current HP is low enough that one bad fight can jeopardize the run; only smith instead when the upgrade is clearly worth more than the survivability gained. Treat the Act 1 floor 15 rest as a model for stabilizing before the boss sequence.
evidence_points: At Act 1 Floor 15, the player was at 39/74 HP and chose rest, healing to 61/74.
The run then reached the Act 1 boss and completed Act 1, later entering the final Act 2 combat at only 26/74 HP.
The final combat ended with the player still alive at 12 HP after three turns, showing how little margin remained when entering the encounter.
reasoning: The Act 1 rest converted a dangerous 39 HP state into a much safer 61 HP state and helped preserve the run through the boss. The same principle should be applied whenever low HP and difficult upcoming fights leave little room for combat variance; the final fight demonstrates the cost of reaching a major encounter with too little buffer.

title: Preserve the final energy for survival when low
situation: When HP is already low, an enemy has an attack intent, and the remaining attack would not kill or decisively change the fight.
lesson: Prefer ending the turn with existing block rather than spending the last energy on marginal damage. In particular, reassess after each attack: if the enemy will still survive and the attack is incoming, retaining block can be more valuable than adding a small amount of damage.
evidence_points: On turn 10 at 18 HP and 8 Block, the agent played Shrug It Off, Cleave, and then Strike on the Acid Slime while it had ATTACK intent; the enemies survived and the next logged state was 2 HP.
On turn 12 at 2 HP, the agent again used Shrug It Off for 6 Block and then spent 2 energy on Bash+ against a 15-HP Spike Slime while another enemy had ATTACK_DEBUFF intent.
reasoning: The turn-10 sequence directly preceded a drop from 18 HP to 2 HP despite having block available. The log does not prove that ending the turn would have survived, but it shows a reusable risk pattern: once survival is the immediate constraint, nonlethal attacks should require a clear payoff before consuming energy that could preserve defensive flexibility.

title: Avoid stacking another defensive card when the deck already has enough block
situation: When a reward offers damage or scaling alongside another block card, and the deck already contains several defensive options.
lesson: Favor cards that improve damage or upgrade key cards rather than taking another broadly defensive card, unless the current deck genuinely cannot survive Act 1 fights. This is especially important before a boss where a long fight can exhaust HP even if the deck blocks reasonably.
evidence_points: At floor 10, the reward offered Armaments and Limit Break alongside Shrug It Off; the agent chose Shrug It Off after already taking Shrug It Off at floor 3.
The final 18-card deck contained 4 Defends, 2 Shrug It Offs, Second Wind, Flame Barrier, Disarm, Sentinel, and only one Perfected Strike as its main scaling-oriented attack choice.
The Slime Boss combat lasted 36 logged decisions and reduced the player from 75 HP at the first logged state to 2 HP near the end.
reasoning: The final deck had substantial defensive coverage but still required a very long boss fight, suggesting that the second Shrug was less valuable than adding damage or improving existing cards. This does not prove Armaments or Limit Break would have won the run, but it supports prioritizing offensive scaling once basic defense is already represented.

title: Keep the pre-boss rest when entering without potions
situation: At the final campfire before an Act 1 boss, when HP is only moderate and the run has no stored potion buffer.
lesson: Rest rather than smithing when the immediate goal is to maximize boss-fight margin and there is no potion reserve. Preserve the earlier smithing opportunity for a healthier campfire, then convert the final campfire into HP.
evidence_points: At floor 6, the agent was at 63/80 HP and chose smithing, upgrading Bash.
At floor 15, the agent was at 51/80 HP and chose rest; the first logged boss-fight state showed 75/80 HP.
The final build had no potions.
reasoning: The sequence used smithing while relatively healthy and then restored HP immediately before the boss, gaining a substantial buffer in a run with no potion safety net. This was a sound preparation pattern worth repeating, even though the later combat decisions still allowed the boss fight to become too long.

title: At critical HP, preserve remaining energy for block
situation: When entering a turn at roughly 5 HP with no block and an enemy attacking next turn, especially if another enemy is only defending or buffing.
lesson: Prioritize a defensive line over marginal damage. In the final fight, after playing Bash+, use the remaining 1 energy on the legal Defend instead of Pommel Strike; do not spend the whole turn attacking while leaving zero block before the enemy attack.
evidence_points: On turn 6, the player had 5/85 HP and 0 block; Centurion intended to defend while Mystic intended to buff, and Defend was a legal alternative, but Bash+ on Mystic was chosen.
After Bash+, the player still had 1 energy and Defend remained legal, but Pommel Strike was chosen instead.
The next logged state showed the player at 5 HP with 0 block while Centurion intended to attack.
reasoning: The logged states show a clear defensive opportunity at the exact decision points. Although the precise incoming damage is unavailable, spending the last energy on offense left no block before an attack while the player had only 5 HP, eliminating survival margin.

title: Match the boss relic to the deck's energy and cost profile
situation: At a boss relic choice when the deck already contains multiple expensive cards and the alternatives include a relic that changes energy/card-play consistency.
lesson: Do not default to a small-value relic such as Tiny House without checking whether the deck needs energy or draw more urgently. With several expensive cards, explicitly compare Snecko Eye's cost reduction and draw against the deck's ability to function with Tiny House.
evidence_points: After the Act 1 boss, Tiny House was chosen over Snecko Eye and Busted Crown.
The final 24-card deck included several expensive cards, including Bash+, Ghostly Armor, Flame Barrier, Pummel, and Feed.
The final relics were Burning Blood, Tiny Chest, Tungsten Rod, and Tiny House; no relic in the final build supplied additional energy or broad combat draw.
reasoning: The final deck's cost profile made energy and draw relevant considerations, while Tiny House supplied only modest value and did not address that constraint. This is an opportunity for more deliberate relic evaluation rather than proof that the choice alone caused the loss.
